props.title: Les Bonnes Femmes

sections.content: Claude Chabrol's **Les Bonnes Femmes** (1960) stands as one of the most unsettling and influential works of the French New Wave, depicting four shop girls in Paris whose dreams of romance lead to devastating consequences. The film's DNA can be traced through later works like **Working Girls** (1986) and **Jeanne Dielman, 23 Quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles** (1975), examining female labor and desire with an unflinching gaze. Chabrol's clinical direction creates an atmosphere of mounting dread beneath seemingly mundane situations, predating similar techniques in **Belle de Jour** (1967) and **The Last Metro** (1980).

sections.content: The film's influence on portraying working women's lives resonates through later European cinema, particularly in works like **L'Argent** (1983) and **Two Days, One Night** (2014). Chabrol's technique of using long takes and precise framing to create psychological tension influenced directors like Michael Haneke and Krzysztof Kieslowski. The shop girls' stories parallel similar themes in **The Umbrellas of Cherbourg** (1964), though Chabrol strips away the musical romanticism for stark realism.

The film's ending, shocking for its time, established a template for feminist critique in cinema that would emerge in works like **Je Tu Il Elle** (1974) and **An Angel at My Table** (1990). Chabrol's attention to class dynamics and social constraints prefigures similar themes in La Ceremonie (1995) and **The Piano Teacher** (2001). SUBHEAD: Impact on Contemporary Cinema

sections.content: Modern filmmakers continue drawing from **Les Bonnes Femmes** (1960). The film's influence can be seen in **4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days** (2007) and **Never Rarely Sometimes Always** (2020), works that examine female friendship and societal constraints with similar clinical precision. The shop setting and exploration of working-class female lives finds echoes in **Carol** (2015) and **Shoplifters** (2018).
